section.title: Paul Accepted by the Apostles
section.sectionRationale: Paul continues his defense by describing his visit to Jerusalem. He set his gospel before the recognized leaders, resisted the demand that Titus be circumcised, and stood firm against false brothers who wanted to enslave the Gentile believers. The pillars added nothing to his gospel and extended the right hand of fellowship. The truth of the gospel was preserved for the Galatians in that very meeting.
section.thesis: When Paul laid his gospel before the Jerusalem leaders, they added nothing to it and recognized the grace given to him, proving that there is one gospel for Jew and Gentile alike, and that the demand to circumcise Gentiles was rejected so that the truth of the gospel might remain.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Paul sets his gospel before the leaders and refuses to have Titus compelled to be circumcised; the false brothers who tried to enslave believers and Paul's refusal to yield; and the pillars recognizing Paul's calling and giving the right hand of fellowship.

units.label: The gospel set before the leaders
units.note: Titus not compelled to be circumcised

verses.text: Fourteen years later I went up again to Jerusalem, accompanied by Barnabas. I took Titus along also.

I went in response to a revelation and set before them the gospel that I preach among the Gentiles. But I spoke privately to those recognized as leaders, for fear that I was running or had already run in vain.
Yet not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek.

units.label: False brothers and the truth of the gospel
units.note: we did not give in for a moment

verses.text: This issue arose because some false brothers had come in under false pretenses to spy on our {{eleutheria|freedom}} in Christ Jesus, in order to enslave us.
We did not give in to them for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you.

units.label: The right hand of fellowship
units.note: the pillars added nothing, only remember the poor

verses.text: But as for the highly esteemed, whatever they were makes no difference to me; God does not show favoritism, those leaders added nothing to me.
On the contrary, they saw that I had been entrusted to preach the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been to the circumcised.
For the One who was at work in Peter's apostleship to the circumcised was also at work in my apostleship to the Gentiles.

And recognizing the {{charis|grace}} that I had been given, James, Cephas, and John, those reputed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of {{koinonia|fellowship}}, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised.
They only asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.

eleutheria.gloss: Freedom, liberty. Here it is the freedom believers have in Christ Jesus, released from the yoke of law keeping as the ground of acceptance with God. The false brothers came precisely to spy out this freedom in order to enslave believers again, which is why Paul would not yield for a moment. Freedom in Christ is a recurring banner of the letter.

koinonia.gloss: Fellowship, partnership, a sharing in common. The right hand of koinonia was a public gesture of recognition and shared mission: the Jerusalem pillars affirmed that Paul and Barnabas preached the same gospel and were partners in the same work, though sent to different peoples. It signals unity of gospel across the divide of Jew and Gentile.

charis.gloss: Grace, God's unearned favor, here also the enabling favor given to Paul for his ministry. The pillars recognized the charis that had been given to Paul, verse 9. His commission to the Gentiles was itself a gift of grace, not a human appointment, which is why they welcomed rather than corrected him.

basic.context: Paul keeps telling his story to prove his gospel is God's. Years after his conversion he went to Jerusalem and laid out the gospel he preached to Gentiles. A test case came up: should Titus, a Greek believer, be circumcised? Paul refused to give in, because the freedom of the gospel was at stake. The leaders recognized God's grace on Paul, added nothing to his message, and shook hands in partnership.
basic.hermeneutics: This is still autobiography serving an argument. The point is twofold: the gospel is one, affirmed by the Jerusalem leaders, and it does not require Gentiles to be circumcised. Read the Titus episode as a deliberate line in the sand: to add circumcision would be to lose the gospel.
basic.originalLanguages: At the center is eleutheria, freedom in Christ, which the false brothers tried to spy out and destroy. The leaders recognized the charis, the grace, given to Paul and offered koinonia, fellowship, a partnership in the one gospel across the Jew and Gentile divide.
basic.typology: The inclusion of the uncircumcised Titus without circumcision anticipates the great truth that in Christ the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile comes down. The one people of God, promised to Abraham as a blessing to all nations, begins to take visible shape as Gentiles are received on the basis of grace alone.
basic.christ: Everything turns on freedom in Christ Jesus. Because Christ has accomplished salvation, acceptance with God rests on Him and not on the badge of circumcision. The same Christ who worked through Peter among Jews worked through Paul among Gentiles, so the one Lord grounds the one gospel.
basic.god: God shows no favoritism, verse 6. He does not measure people by status or reputation, and He entrusts the gospel to whom He wills. It is God who was at work in both Peter and Paul, and it is the grace of God that the pillars recognized. The unity of the mission rests on the one God who saves by grace.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 15 records the Jerusalem council settling the circumcision question. Ephesians 2 says Christ has broken down the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile. Acts 10 shows God accepting Gentiles apart from the law.
basic.oneStory: God promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed through him. Here that promise advances: Gentiles are welcomed on the basis of grace, without becoming Jews first. The one gospel unites a divided humanity, a preview of the new people God is gathering in Christ.

context.literary:
The second chapter continues the autobiography begun in 1:11, and these ten verses are the heart of it. The pattern of the narrative is a tension that is raised and released. Verses 1 and 2 introduce the journey and a private meeting, with a fear voiced aloud, that Paul might be running or have run in vain. Verses 3 to 5 raise the stakes with Titus and the false brothers. Verses 6 to 10 resolve it with the leaders' recognition and handshake.

The Greek of the passage is notoriously rough. Verses 3 to 5 are not a smooth sentence but a series of broken constructions. Sentences begin, break off and restart, and a reader can feel him pressing on while the grammar gives out. Verse 6 has the same character: 'those who seemed to be something' begins a thought that is interrupted by a parenthesis, 'whatever they were makes no difference to me,' and is only completed in a new form. Paul is writing with heat. The rough edges give the section the sound of a man who is still angry about what nearly happened.

The structure also repeats a pair of key terms. The word for 'recognised' or 'esteemed' is used three times, in verses 2, 6 and 9, and its final use is the one that names the 'pillars.' Paul seems to be playing with it: they were counted as important, and he will not deny it, but the weight of their reputation does not decide the matter. In the middle of the passage, verse 5, stands the phrase that gives the whole chapter its aim, 'the truth of the gospel.'

The movement from 'I' to 'we' to 'they' is also deliberate. Paul goes up alone with Barnabas and Titus, 'we' resist the false brothers, and 'they' extend the right hand. By verse 10 the singular returns: 'the very thing I was eager to do.'
context.historical:
The visit in Galatians 2:1 came 'fourteen years later,' and the phrase is ambiguous about the starting point. It may count from his conversion or from the earlier Jerusalem visit of 1:18. Either way, the visit took place roughly in the middle of the forties of the first century. Barnabas, a Cypriot Levite and an early leader of the church, went with him, and Titus was taken along, a Greek believer who may have been converted through Paul.

Circumcision was at that point the issue that most clearly marked who belonged to the people of God. It was a command given to Abraham, Genesis 17, and it had been defended at great cost under the Maccabees. For many Jewish Christians, to be saved meant entering the family of Abraham, and that entailed circumcision. Acts shows how the church first came to this question in Antioch when men came down from Judea and taught that unless the brothers were circumcised they could not be saved, Acts 15:1-2. Paul's visit here is a resolution of that kind of dispute.

The three men Paul calls pillars were James, Cephas and John. James, the Lord's brother, led the Jerusalem church, and Peter and John were two of the Twelve. The term 'pillars' was a title of honour for those who bore the weight of the church, and Paul uses it with a measure of reserve.

The 'false brothers' who came in 'under false pretenses' are described in the language of espionage. Their purpose was to observe the freedom Gentile believers enjoyed and to draw them back under the law. The request at the end, to remember the poor, refers to the poverty of the Jerusalem church. Paul spent years collecting funds from the Gentile churches for them, 1 Corinthians 16:1-4 and Romans 15:25-27, and he mentions that he told the Galatians to join in the collection, so they had been taught about it.
context.canonical:
The question of circumcision runs from Abraham to Paul. It begins with a covenant sign given to Abraham and his household, including foreigners born in his house, Genesis 17:9-14. The prophets spoke of a circumcision of the heart, so that the outward mark had always pointed to an inward reality. Paul builds on that in Romans 2:28-29, where the true Jew is one inwardly, and in Romans 4:11-12, where Abraham was counted righteous while still uncircumcised, so that he might be the father of all who believe, whether circumcised or not.

The passage anticipates the council recorded in Acts 15, where Peter reminds the assembly that God gave the Spirit to the Gentiles and made no distinction between them and the Jews, cleansing their hearts by faith, Acts 15:7-11. James then gives the judgment that no trouble should be made for the Gentiles who turn to God, Acts 15:19. Behind both lies the earlier story of Cornelius, where Peter says 'God does not show favoritism,' Acts 10:34. Paul's own phrase in verse 6, that God does not show favoritism, belongs to the same line and goes back to Deuteronomy 10:17, which says the Lord shows no partiality.

The teaching of Galatians 2 gets its fullest development in the rest of the letter, particularly Galatians 3:28 and 5:2-6, where Paul says that in Christ neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, and that faith working through love is what matters. Ephesians 2:14-16 adds that Christ has torn down the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile and made the two into one new man, and Philippians 3:3 and Colossians 2:11 apply the circumcision language to believers directly.

The concern for the poor reaches back to Deuteronomy 15:11, where the command to open the hand to the poor is renewed because the poor will never cease from the land.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul tells this story to show how the Jerusalem leaders treated his gospel when they heard it, because the Galatians had been told that Jerusalem disagreed with him. The agitators evidently presented themselves as friends of the apostles. Paul's reply is that when the apostles actually sat with him, they added nothing. They did not ask for Titus to be circumcised, they did not revise his message, and they gave him the right hand of fellowship.

He also wants them to see what was at stake. The Titus episode is a test case, and Paul will not let it be reduced to a question of custom. If a Gentile believer had to be circumcised in order to be fully accepted, the gospel would no longer be a gospel of grace. 'We did not give in to them for a moment,' he says, 'so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you.' The Galatians are the ones he is protecting.

Another aim is to put the matter of reputation in its place. Paul does not deny that the pillars were important. But verse 6 says plainly that their status makes no difference to him because God does not show favouritism. He is not trying to humble the apostles. He is asking his readers not to weigh a message by the prestige of its bearer. This is the same point he made in 1:8, when he said that even an angel from heaven would not alter the case.

He ends by pointing out the shared concern for the poor. The one thing the leaders asked was something he was already eager to do. By saying this, he shows that the two missions are different in focus but one in heart.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is an account of what happened in a meeting. It is not a command to refuse every leader's request or to resist every authority. Paul resisted a particular demand, the circumcision of Titus, because yielding would have given up the truth of the gospel. The same Paul later circumcised Timothy, Acts 16:3, for the sake of the Jews in that area. The difference lies in the principle at stake: in Titus's case the demand was made as a requirement for acceptance, and in Timothy's case it was a voluntary act of respect in a mixed setting.

What carries over to the present is the principle that nothing should be added to Christ as a requirement for belonging to God's people. Churches today face their own versions of the Titus case. Whenever a practice, background or tradition is made a condition of full acceptance, the question of Galatians 2 is being asked again.

The passage also shows how to hold unity and truth together. Paul stood his ground and also received the pillars' hand. The partnership was possible because the gospel itself was agreed. The request to remember the poor is a standing command, and the passage models the church's care for those in need as a mark of gospel life. It is described as something Paul was already eager to do, so it is a response to grace and not a payment for acceptance.

debates.question: How does this Jerusalem visit fit with the book of Acts?

views.label: The council visit of Acts 15
views.case: Many take Galatians 2:1-10 as the same meeting as Acts 15. In both, Paul and Barnabas go up to Jerusalem to deal with the question of circumcising Gentiles, and the leaders include Peter and James. On this view the letter was written after the council.

views.label: The famine visit of Acts 11
views.case: Others match it with Acts 11:27-30, when Barnabas and Saul brought relief to the believers in Judea. They note that Paul says he went 'in response to a revelation,' which fits Agabus's prophecy of a famine, and that the council in Acts 15 would otherwise be oddly missing from Paul's account, since it would have settled the argument at once. This view usually goes with the southern Galatia theory and an early date.

debates.bearing: The two views disagree about the letter's date but not about its message. In both cases, the leaders affirmed that Gentiles do not need circumcision, and in both the unity of the gospel is the point. The reader should hold the matter with some humility, since Luke and Paul are each selecting what serves their purpose.

debates.question: Did Paul give in on Titus for a time or refuse completely?

views.label: He refused entirely
views.case: Verse 3 says Titus was not compelled to be circumcised, and verse 5 says 'We did not give in to them for a moment.' The most natural reading is that Titus was not circumcised and that Paul's refusal was deliberate.

views.label: Some suggest Titus was circumcised voluntarily
views.case: A few early Western witnesses omit the negative in verse 5, which would yield 'to whom we yielded for an hour.' Some readers take this as Paul having agreed in order to avoid scandal. The wording of the main manuscripts and the flow of the argument, in which Paul stresses that even a Greek was not compelled, do not support it.

debates.bearing: The great majority of readers take Titus to have been left uncircumcised, because Paul's argument depends on it. The point is not that circumcision is wrong in itself, but that it cannot be made a requirement, and that to make it one is to lose the truth of the gospel.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 uses the verb anatithemi, in the middle voice, for 'set before them.' It means to lay something out for consideration and carries a sense of putting a case on the table. Paul did not go to ask for permission but to place the gospel in view, which is why the next clause can say that he spoke privately to those 'recognised as leaders.' The participle there, dokountes, is the word 'those who seem' or 'those who are held in esteem.' It recurs in verse 6 and again in verse 9, with the added word 'pillars,' stuloi. Paul's repeated use has a note of detachment. He grants the esteem and notes that it does not decide the question.

The same verse contains the fear that he might be running 'in vain,' eis kenon. The word kenon means empty, and the image of a runner whose race comes to nothing is one Paul uses elsewhere, Philippians 2:16. It does not mean that Paul doubted his gospel. It means that disunity with Jerusalem could have emptied his work of its effect, and so the Gentile mission needed the recognition of the whole church.

In verse 4 the false brothers are 'pseudadelphoi,' a word Paul also uses in 2 Corinthians 11:26, and he says they were 'smuggled in,' pareisaktoi, and came in alongside, pareiselthon, 'to spy out,' kataskopesai, the freedom of the believers. The last verb is the one for a scout surveying an enemy position. The intended result is stated with the verb katadouloo, to bring into complete slavery, a stronger form of the plain verb for making someone a slave.

Verse 5 says Paul did not 'give in,' eixamen, to them 'in submission,' te hypotage, and that he held firm so that 'the truth of the gospel,' he aletheia tou euangeliou, might remain, diameine, with them. The verb has the sense of staying through to the end. Paul sees the gospel as something that must be kept and that can be lost.

In verse 6, 'God does not show favoritism' translates a Greek phrase that means literally 'God does not receive the face of a man,' prosopon ho theos anthropou ou lambanei. It reflects the Hebrew idiom of lifting the face, and is the opposite of showing partiality.

Verse 8 uses the verb energeo twice, for God's active working: the One who 'was at work,' energesas, in Peter was also 'at work,' energesen, in Paul. In verse 9, koinonia is paired with 'right hands,' dexias, the gesture of agreement. Finally, in verse 10 the verb for 'remember' is in the present tense, mnemoneuomen, a standing practice, and Paul says he was 'eager,' espoudasa, to do it, an aorist that points to a past decision.

typology.type: Circumcision as the sign of the covenant, Genesis 17:9-14
typology.fulfillment: The command to Abraham marked every male in his household, including foreigners born or bought, as belonging to God's covenant people. The correspondence is that the sign marks who is within the family. In Christ the sign gives way to what it signified: the circumcision of the heart, Romans 2:29, and the circumcision made by Christ and not by human hands, Colossians 2:11. The type falls short because the physical mark could be given to someone without faith, while the reality it pointed to is given only through the Spirit.

typology.type: The wall between Israel and the nations
typology.fulfillment: The law's boundaries kept Israel distinct, and the temple had a court beyond which Gentiles could not go. Titus, a Gentile welcomed without circumcision, stands at the beginning of the change that Ephesians 2:14-16 describes: Christ has torn down the dividing wall and made the two one new man. The type falls short in that the wall was a God given protection for a time, so its fall is not a loss but a completion, as Galatians 3:23-25 will explain.

typology.type: The pillars of the temple and the church
typology.fulfillment: James, Cephas and John are called pillars, a word that recalls the pillars of the temple and the image of the house of God. In Christ the dwelling of God is a people, and the church is called a household 'built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone,' Ephesians 2:20. The correspondence is of a structure carried by persons. The type falls short in that Christ alone is the foundation, and Paul's cool tone toward the title shows that status among the apostles carries no weight with God.

study.christ:
The phrase that governs this passage is 'our freedom in Christ Jesus,' verse 4. It is a freedom located in a person. Everything the false brothers wanted to impose is measured against that. To say that freedom is in Christ is to say that the believer's standing does not depend on any list of observances, any badge or any lineage, but on being united to the Lord who is the end of the law for those who believe, as Romans 10:4 says.

The passage presses a particular claim: Christ is enough. If Titus had been circumcised under compulsion, it would have said that something more than union with Christ was needed to be fully a member of God's people. Paul sees that this would have emptied the cross, and he says as much later: 'if righteousness comes through the law, Christ died for nothing,' Galatians 2:21. This is why he will not give way for a moment. The freedom at stake is the freedom Christ purchased.

Verse 8 also shows Christ at work in the mission. 'The One who was at work in Peter's apostleship to the circumcised was also at work in my apostleship to the Gentiles.' The one at work is the risen Lord, acting through His servants. The Jerusalem leaders saw the same Christ in both missions. Peter preached to Jews and Paul to Gentiles, but the Lord of both was one, and so was the gospel.

There is a theme of Christ and the poor too. The leaders' only request was that Paul remember the poor. In the same letter, Paul will tell the Galatians that the Son of God 'loved me and gave Himself up for me,' 2:20. A gospel that begins in the self-giving of Christ cannot be indifferent to those in need. He is the one who 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. The care for the poor is a family likeness.

The passage is also a reminder that the unity of the church comes from Christ and is expressed in fellowship. The right hand of fellowship was given because both sides recognised the same grace and the same Lord. It is the visible form of the unity Jesus prayed for, 'that all of them may be one,' John 17:21.
study.god:
This passage shows God as impartial. Verse 6 says that God does not show favoritism, and Paul puts the words to work against reputation. The leaders were highly esteemed, but God does not rank His servants by status. He looks at the heart and works through whom He chooses. The idea is rooted in the law, 'the LORD your God... showing no partiality,' Deuteronomy 10:17, and Peter shares it in Acts 10:34. This impartiality is the ground of the Gentile mission: if God does not receive faces, then He can receive Gentiles on the same terms as Jews.

God is also the one who works. Verse 8 describes Him as active in two apostleships at once, 'at work in Peter's apostleship... also at work in my apostleship.' The mission is not the product of human strategy but of the One who energises it. This gives the church confidence that the mission will succeed, and humility, because the credit belongs to God.

He is faithful to His gospel. The truth of the gospel is a deposit that God watches over, and Paul's refusal to yield is an act of trust in a God who keeps His promise through grace. The God who promised to bless all nations through Abraham, Genesis 12:3, is the same God now receiving Gentiles through faith, with no condition attached.

He is a God of grace. In verse 9 the leaders recognised 'the grace that I had been given,' and that is what persuaded them. They did not first examine Paul's credentials, nor did they test his theology against a checklist. They saw grace at work. The God of grace shows Himself in what He does in people.

He is a God who cares for the poor. Deuteronomy 15:11 and Proverbs 19:17 both treat generosity to the poor as something the Lord notices, and the leaders' request in verse 10 is of a piece with that. Worship that shuts out the poor is not the worship of this God.

For the life of the church this means that unity is a gift of God that must be guarded. The church should test its leaders by the gospel, not by status, receive whom God has received, and match its theology with its generosity.

crossReferences.note: Men from Judea taught that unless the brothers were circumcised they could not be saved, and Paul and Barnabas were sent to Jerusalem about it. This is the controversy behind Galatians 2:1-5, whether the visit is the same or a close relative.

Peter's speech at the council says God gave the Holy Spirit to the Gentiles and made no distinction between them and the Jews. It is the apostolic ground for what the pillars recognised in Paul's work, and it ends on salvation by grace for all.

Barnabas and Saul take relief to the elders in Judea during a famine. It is the other candidate for the visit of Galatians 2, and it is the earliest instance of the care for the poor named in verse 10.
Paul circumcises Timothy, whose mother was Jewish and whose father was Greek, because of the Jews in that area. Set beside Titus, it shows that the issue was compulsion, not the operation itself.

Peter later withdraws from eating with Gentiles for fear of the circumcision group, and Paul opposes him because he was not walking in line with the truth of the gospel. It shows that the agreement of verse 9 had to be defended in practice.

The covenant of circumcision given to Abraham, including those born in his household or bought from a foreigner. It is the text the agitators leaned on, and the one Paul must answer in Galatians 3 and 4.
Christ has made the two one and torn down the dividing wall of hostility. It is the larger picture of which Titus, welcomed without circumcision, is an early and living case.

Paul says that if the Galatians let themselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to them, and that what matters is faith expressed through love. It is the full statement of the principle at stake in the refusal over Titus.

Paul describes the contribution Macedonia and Achaia made for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem, and says that Gentiles who share in spiritual blessings owe material help. It is the long fruit of the request in Galatians 2:10.

Paul tells the Corinthians to do as he directed the churches of Galatia, setting aside money weekly for the saints. It shows that the Galatians were part of the collection and that the request of verse 10 was carried out.
Peter learns that God does not show favoritism and welcomes people from every nation who fear Him. It is the same truth Paul states in verse 6, learned by Peter himself before the council.

Paul calls Titus his partner and fellow worker among the Corinthians. The man who was not compelled to be circumcised became one of Paul's trusted colleagues, proof that the freedom defended in Galatians 2 bore fruit.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's promise to Abraham was always larger than one nation. God said that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3, and yet the sign of his covenant, circumcision, marked off his physical family. This tension runs through the Old Testament as the prophets speak of nations streaming to Zion and of a heart circumcised by God. Galatians 2:1-10 is one of the places where the tension is settled in public. A Greek man stands among the apostles, accepted without the sign, and the leaders of the church say that nothing needs to be added.

Looking back, the passage answers the question of how Gentiles could ever be part of God's people. The answer is not that they become Jews first. The answer is that the promise to Abraham is fulfilled in Christ and given to all who believe. The law had a time and a purpose, but now that the seed has come, as Galatians 3 will say, the sign of belonging is faith and not flesh.

Looking forward, the passage points to the new humanity that Ephesians describes, one body of Jew and Gentile reconciled to God through the cross, Ephesians 2:16. It also points to the church of the nations in the book of Revelation, where a great multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language stands before the throne, Revelation 7:9. The truth Paul defended for the Galatians is the same truth that makes that multitude possible. If the gospel had been bent to require circumcision, that multitude could not have been gathered from every nation.

The passage also holds a lesson in how God's people live in the meantime. The partnership of Paul and the pillars is a picture of the church's unity in diversity. There are different missions, to the circumcised and to the Gentiles, but the same Lord and the same gospel. The shared concern for the poor is the visible mark of that unity, and the collection that followed was the practical bond between Jewish and Gentile believers.

The story ends where Scripture ends, with God dwelling among His people from all nations, Revelation 21:3. The right hand of fellowship in Jerusalem was a small foretaste of that fellowship.

sermon.title: At Stake: The Truth of the Gospel (Galatians 2:1 to 10)
sermon.why: Begg shows how the truth of the gospel itself was at stake in the Jerusalem meeting, why Paul refused to compromise over Titus, and how the leaders recognized the one gospel of grace for Jew and Gentile alike.

quiz.q: Why would Paul not allow Titus to be compelled to be circumcised?

options.text: Because the freedom and truth of the gospel were at stake.
options.note: To require circumcision would add to grace and enslave believers.

options.text: Because circumcision was physically dangerous.
options.note: The issue was theological, not medical.

options.text: Because Titus personally disliked the idea.
options.note: The refusal defended the gospel, not merely a preference.

options.text: Because Paul opposed all Jewish customs.
options.note: Paul did not oppose the customs themselves, only imposing them as a condition of salvation.

quiz.q: Who were the false brothers, and what did they want?

options.text: Infiltrators who spied on the believers' freedom in order to enslave them.
options.note: Verse 4 describes their aim to re-impose the law's yoke.

options.text: Sincere teachers with a slightly different emphasis.
options.note: Paul calls them false brothers with false pretenses, not sincere teachers.

options.text: Roman officials investigating the church.
options.note: They came in as pretended brothers, not civil authorities.

options.text: Gentile believers resisting the apostles.
options.note: They pushed law keeping on Gentiles, the opposite of resisting it.

quiz.q: What did the Jerusalem pillars add to Paul's gospel?

options.text: Nothing; they recognized his calling and gave the right hand of fellowship.
options.note: Verses 6 and 9 stress they added nothing and affirmed him.

options.text: A requirement that Gentiles keep the whole law.
options.note: The opposite; they did not impose the law on Gentiles.

options.text: A demand that Paul stop preaching to Gentiles.
options.note: They sent him to the Gentiles with their blessing.

options.text: A rebuke for preaching without permission.
options.note: They welcomed him as a partner, not a rogue.

quiz.q: What does verse 6 say about God's view of status?

options.text: God does not show favoritism.
options.note: Human reputation carries no weight with God.

options.text: God favors those with the highest standing.
options.note: The verse says the opposite; He shows no favoritism.

options.text: God prefers the poor over the influential.
options.note: The point is impartiality, not a reversed favoritism.

options.text: God judges people by their titles.
options.note: Titles make no difference to God.

quiz.q: What one thing did the pillars ask Paul to remember?

options.text: The poor, which Paul was already eager to do.
options.note: Verse 10 records the single request, care for the poor.

options.text: To keep the food laws carefully.
options.note: No such requirement was added; only remembering the poor.

options.text: To send money to the apostles personally.
options.note: The concern was the poor, not the apostles' income.

options.text: To stop associating with Gentiles.
options.note: They affirmed his mission to the Gentiles.

questions: Paul refused to give in even for a moment when the truth of the gospel was at stake. Where might faithfulness require you to hold a clear line rather than compromise?
The pillars recognized the grace God had given Paul rather than his status. How well do you discern God's work in people regardless of their reputation?
Freedom in Christ was worth defending against those who would enslave believers again. What forms of religious slavery are you tempted to return to?
The one request was to remember the poor. How does caring for the poor fit with a robust commitment to the gospel of grace?
God shows no favoritism. How might that truth reshape the way your church welcomes people who are different from you?

translationNotes.note: God does not show favoritism translates a Hebraic idiom, literally God does not accept the face of man.
Cephas is the Aramaic name for Peter.
The right hand of fellowship renders koinonia, a public gesture of shared partnership in the one gospel, sending Paul to the Gentiles and the pillars to the circumcised.
